ACCENT_STATUS_HUE_SEPARATION
#

theme_validate.ts view source

20 import {ACCENT_STATUS_HUE_SEPARATION} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_validate.js';

How far in degrees the accent hue has to sit from each status hue before validate_theme stops warning. At the chroma links and labels render at, 12 degrees reads as one color with a shift (a red accent beside the default orange caution) while 30 reads as two (a pink accent beside the default red negative), so the threshold sits between them. The defaults' closest accent and status pair, blue and cyan, is 40 degrees apart.

apply_theme_variables
#

variable_graph.ts view source

(variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[], theme: ResolvedTheme | null | undefined): { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[] import {apply_theme_variables} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/variable_graph.js';

Overlays a baked theme onto a resolved variable set, last-wins by name.

This is how a theme is baked in at build time: the overlaid values flow through the dependency graph like any other, so the variables a theme references are pulled in transitively and the output stays tree-shaken. The overlay follows render_theme_style's order - the stance mirror (minus the names the theme or its caps set), then the theme's own variables (minus any internal name, which a theme can't set), then the caps. A slot the stylesheet can't hold is dropped before it overlays, as render_theme_style drops it, so the value beneath it stays.

variables

the resolved default or custom variables

type StyleVariable[]

theme

the baked theme to overlay (see bake_theme), or null/undefined for none

type ResolvedTheme | null | undefined

returns

StyleVariable[]

the composed variables, or variables unchanged when there's no theme

bake_theme
#

variable_graph.ts view source

(theme: { name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; } | ResolvedTheme, variables: { ...; }[], diagnostics?: GenerationDiagnostic[] | undefined): ResolvedTheme import {bake_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/variable_graph.js';

Derives what a build-time theme renders with from the configured variable set: the stance mirror, re-slotted from the configured variables (so a build that customizes a scheme-adaptive variable mirrors its own value, not the default), and the caps compute_theme_caps recomputes for the theme's hues and lightness - the derived half of compile_theme. A ResolvedTheme passed in has its theme baked the same way - a supplied mirror or caps are recomputed, so the output can't depend on derived data computed against another variable set or an older release.

The theme's variables pass the containment checks first, as build_variable_graph applies them: a slot the stylesheet can't hold, or an entry without a plain-identifier name, is reported as an uncontained_theme_value error and left out, and the caps, the gates, and the overlay all see the contained theme - what renders.

The caps and the gates measure the theme over the configured set: a knob-tier value (theme_knobs) the configured variables change from the default is folded in beneath the theme's own, re-slotted for a stance as the mirror re-slots it, so a build that retunes a ramp knob is capped and gated at what it renders. A configured value the gates can't read lands in unchecked.

The gates (check_theme with the caps) report as warnings, since a theme can knowingly give up a gate: theme_gate_failed lists the failing gate entries and theme_gate_unchecked the inputs the gates couldn't evaluate. A stanced theme renders its one appearance in both schemes, so only the stanced scheme's entries are listed. The lint (validate_theme) runs over the contained theme, so a slot reported as uncontained isn't reported again: each issue is a theme_lint diagnostic at the issue's level, so an unknown variable fails a build that throws on errors.

theme

the configured theme option

type Theme | ResolvedTheme

variables

the configured variable set the theme overlays

type StyleVariable[]

diagnostics?

collects the containment errors, the lint issues, and the gate warnings, when given

type GenerationDiagnostic[]
optional

returns

ResolvedTheme

the contained wire theme with its mirror and caps

Alpha (in %) of each border color stop. A perceptually-uniform curve - small gaps at the low end, large at the high end - boosted at the low end in dark mode where borders are less visible against dark backgrounds. Stop 00 renders transparent and stop 100 opaque.

check_theme
#

theme_check.ts view source

(theme: { name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }, options?: ThemeResolverOptions): ThemeCheckReport import {check_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_check.js';

Runs the gamut, monotonicity, and contrast gates against a theme, resolving its authored CSS back to numbers through the resolution core. Report-only: failures land in entries (with pass: false), inputs that can't be evaluated land in unchecked, and ok is true only when every entry passes and nothing is unchecked. Never throws.

Every color a gate reads is looked up by its variable name, so a theme that authors one directly - a stop (palette_a_50, shade_00, text_max, border_color_30) or a role (text_color, link_color, border_color) - is measured at the authored color when it is an oklch(L C H) numeric literal or an exact var() reference to another color the gates evaluate, and recorded in unchecked otherwise. An authored color a gate depends on never passes unread, and one no gate reads stays out of the report.

A contrast subject names what was measured: the default stop while a role is at its default (text_80 on shade_00), the role once the theme authors it (text_color on shade_00).

An intent stop that renders the same color as a palette letter's (the default for every intent) folds into that letter's gamut entry rather than duplicating it, so reports for letter-bound themes list fewer subjects than the full letters × intents grid.

theme

the theme to check

type Theme

options

the compiled caps to check the theme with, as compute_theme_caps returns them

type ThemeResolverOptions
default {}

returns

CHROMA_STOP_CSS_MATCHER
#

ramps.ts view source

internal

Shared by `variable.ts` and `theme_resolver.ts` - not stable API.

RegExp import {CHROMA_STOP_CSS_MATCHER} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Matches the capped form render_chroma_stop_css emits, capturing the stop and the cap - how the resolver reads a compiled cap back, and how the Theme schema admits the one intermediate a theme can carry (see StyleVariable). It admits CSS whitespace only, around the value and inside it, so a match needs no trim() (which, like \s, takes U+00A0).

ChromaRampKnobs
#

ramps.ts view source

ChromaRampKnobs import type {ChromaRampKnobs} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Knobs for the symmetric mid-peaked chroma curve, C(t) = min + (max - min) * pow(4t(1-t), curve). The curve expresses the *request*; rendered stops are clamped by PALETTE_CHROMA_CAPS per stop, and --chroma_scale multiplies above the clamp (so vivid themes can knowingly push past the caps and gamut-clip).

chroma_min

Chroma requested at the ramp endpoints (stops 00/100), before capping.

type number

chroma_max

Chroma requested at the ramp midpoint (stop 50), before capping.

type number

curve

Falloff exponent of the peak; higher concentrates chroma at the middle.

type number

compose_themes
#

theme.ts view source

(base: { name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }, ...overlays: { ...; }[]): { ...; } import {compose_themes} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme.js';

Composes a base theme with overlay fragments by flatten + last-wins: later variables replace same-named earlier ones wholesale, a dark-only overlay keeping the base slot beneath it (see overlay_style_variable). Any knob-only theme is already a valid fragment - the contrast modifiers in contrast_modifiers are the canonical overlays. This is the hand-flatten precursor to a first-class extends, with the same merge semantics.

The base's scheme stance wins; when the base is single-scheme, each overlay variable is re-slotted to the stanced scheme's value so a dual-slot fragment can't leak the other scheme's appearance past the stance. The result is a plain theme like its inputs - resolve it to render a stance faithfully. The composed name appends the overlay names so name-keyed pickers and renderers treat the composition as its own theme, and the base's summary carries through.

returns

(theme: { name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }): { ...; }[] import {compute_theme_caps} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_check.js';

Recomputes a theme's per-stop worst-hue chroma caps from its own hues and the palette lightness each stop resolves to, then returns _palette_chroma_NN caps wherever the baked ones no longer fit - the fix for a theme (rotated hues, a monochrome collapse, a moved lightness ramp) whose gamut headroom the baked worst-hue table misjudges. The caps are derived data beside the theme, never in it: a theme can't set an internal variable, so they render through render_theme_style's caps option and recomputing them for the same theme gives the same caps.

Each stop's cap is computed at the lightness the resolution core resolves for the stop in that scheme - the theme's endpoint-and-curve ramp - so the caps describe the same colors check_theme gates.

A stop is emitted when either scheme's recomputed cap is tighter than the baked value, or looser by more than the emit epsilon. Nothing is emitted when a hue fails to resolve to a number, since caps computed without it could overshoot its gamut, and a stop whose lightness fails to resolve is skipped. An override emits both slots together, so a one-scheme override can't silently kill the base default's other slot by cascade-layer order, collapsing to a single slot in the base position when the two rendered values coincide.

A stanced theme's two schemes resolve to the stanced appearance through the mirror, so its caps are baselined against the stanced scheme's baked table - the values the mirror already re-slots - and a stance alone (hues and lightness unmoved) emits nothing. Its overrides coincide across schemes and emit single-slot unless the theme authors a dark slot that splits them.

The caps bound the requested chroma only: chroma_scale and the per-slot *_chroma_scale multipliers apply above the clamp. A theme that raises one past 1 clips by design - its gamut failures survive the compile, and a cap the compile loosens can add to them, since the multiplier then pushes more stops past the looser cap. Gate the theme with them through check_theme(theme, {caps}).

theme

the theme to recompute caps for

type Theme

returns

StyleVariable[]

the _palette_chroma_NN caps that moved, empty when the baked ones all still fit

compute_worst_hue_chroma_cap
#

ramps.ts view source

(hues: readonly number[], lightness: number): number import {compute_worst_hue_chroma_cap} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Computes the worst-hue safe chroma cap at one lightness: the minimum oklch_max_srgb_chroma across the hues, floored to 4 decimals to stay conservative (the browser clips anything past it). The generalization of the baked PALETTE_CHROMA_CAPS to an arbitrary hue set and lightness - a theme's compile step calls it with each stop's own resolved lightness to detect where the baked worst-hue envelope no longer fits.

hues

OKLCH hue angles the stop must stay in gamut for

lightness

contrast_modifiers
#

themes.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }[]

type Theme[]

import {contrast_modifiers} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes.js';

The contrast modifiers: small axis fragments composed over any theme via compose_themes rather than picked as themes themselves. Composition is flatten + last-wins, so a modifier's variables replace the base theme's same-named ones - a base that moves the same knobs cedes them to the modifier. Both move the shade endpoint (shade_lightness_00), since contrast is the ground-to-text range, so a theme whose identity is its ground yields it. High contrast also bends the text curve (text_lightness_curve) and sets border_color to a stop that holds a control's boundary against a ground its fill can no longer separate from

  • a base with its own border_color cedes it like any other variable,

stronger rules included. Neither touches the neutral cast, which stays the theme's.

CoreReason
#

style_rule_parser.ts view source

CoreReason

type "universal" | "root" | "body" | "conditional_core" | "html" | "host" | "at_rule" | "untargetable"

import type {CoreReason} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/style_rule_parser.js';

Reasons a rule is considered "core" and always included. conditional_core marks a conditional group rule (@media, @supports, @container) that contains something which always ships on its own - a core rule or an at_rule. at_rule marks every at-rule that is not a conditional group (@keyframes, @font-face, @property, @scope, ...): detection has no way to tell whether one is used, so it ships as written. untargetable marks rules with a selector the index can't match - one that names no element or class at all (pseudo-element or attribute selectors like ::selection and [hidden]), or one with an escaped or non-ASCII identifier (.md\:flex, .café) - so tree-shaking would drop them whether or not the project uses them.

css_class_composites
#

css_class_composites.ts view source

Record<string, CssClassDefinition | undefined>

type Record<string, CssClassDefinition | undefined>

import {css_class_composites} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_composites.js';

The builtin composite classes. The multi-property ones render in the fuz.utilities.composites sublayer (composite: true, the default for rulesets), so a token or literal class on the same element wins over them; the single-property shortcuts (circular, pixelated, mb_flow, mt_flow) are single-purpose and order with the token classes. Their forced-colors rules nest inside their own rules (`@media (forced-colors: active)`), so a modified variant keeps them conditional, and a browser without CSS nesting, which also has no forced-colors mode, skips them.

Checks that a declaration value can't end its own declaration or rule: quotes and brackets balance, and nothing outside a string closes the declaration (a top-level ;), opens or closes a block, sets !important, opens a comment, or escapes a character. Stricter than the grammar where that keeps the rule simple - braces, comments, and escapes outside strings are rejected outright, as is an unquoted url( whose contents a quoted one would hold, so quote a URL that needs them.

CssClassDefinitionBase

css_class_generation.ts view source

CssClassDefinitionBase import type {CssClassDefinitionBase} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_generation.js';

comment?

type string

composite?

Whether the class is a composite, rendered in the fuz.utilities.composites sublayer beneath every single-purpose class, so a token or literal class on the same element always wins over the composite's declaration of the same property. Defaults to true for composes and ruleset definitions, false for a declaration without composes.

type boolean

late?

Whether the class orders late within its bucket: after every rule that ties with it on color scheme, media query, property rank, and state order, interpreted literals included, so display:flex hidden hides while a media query still outranks it (hidden md:flex shows at md and up). For an override that should win its ties whatever else names the same property, like hidden. Composites order by their registry position, which no two share, so the flag only reorders single-purpose classes.

type boolean

CssClassDefinitionInterpreter

css_class_generation.ts view source

CssClassDefinitionInterpreter import type {CssClassDefinitionInterpreter} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_generation.js';

Interpreter for dynamic CSS class generation based on pattern matching.

An interpreter sees a class name with its modifiers already stripped - md:hover:grid-cols-4 reaches it as grid-cols-4 - and returns a definition like a static one, so modifiers, ordering, and layering apply to what it returns the same as to a static class. A ruleset names the class it was given; the generator renames it to the full modified class. What an interpreter returns renders verbatim, so containing values built from class names found in markup is the interpreter's job.

Leading segments named like modifiers are stripped greedily, and the generator backs off one at a time, so an interpreter is offered the shortest base first: marker:none arrives as none before the full literal, since marker is also a pseudo-element modifier (cue likewise). A broad pattern shouldn't claim such a sub-base.

CssClassOptions
#

css_plugin_options.ts view source

CssClassOptions import type {CssClassOptions} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_plugin_options.js';

Options for CSS class definitions and interpretation. Controls how classes are defined and how dynamic classes are generated.

class_definitions?

Class definitions, merged over the default token and composite classes as a record, or a callback over the defaults returning the whole set. A record's definition takes precedence over a default with the same name.

Registry order breaks ties between single-purpose classes of equal rank, and for composites it is their order, so where a definition lands matters: one with a new name is ordered after the defaults, so it beats a built-in token it ties with on the same property (though not a literal like padding:0, which orders after every static definition), while one overriding a default's name keeps that default's position. A callback's result is the registry in the order it returns, and a callback that doesn't return an object fails generator creation.

type Record<string, CssClassDefinition | undefined> | ((defaults: Record<string, CssClassDefinition | undefined>) => Record<string, CssClassDefinition | undefined>)

// add composites over the defaults class_definitions: custom_composites // only your own definitions, none of the defaults class_definitions: () => custom_composites

class_interpreters?

Interpreters for dynamic class generation, replacing the builtin interpreters as an array, or a callback over them. The builtins are the CSS-literal interpreter, so keep them to keep literal classes.

A callback that doesn't return an array fails generator creation.

type CssClassDefinitionInterpreter[] | ((defaults: CssClassDefinitionInterpreter[]) => CssClassDefinitionInterpreter[])

// run a custom interpreter before the CSS-literal one class_interpreters: (defaults) => [grid_cols_interpreter, ...defaults]

CssDiagnosticsOptions import type {CssDiagnosticsOptions} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_plugin_options.js';

Options for error and warning handling.

on_error?

How to handle errors during generation: unresolvable comment hints, invalid CSS literals, and the base stylesheet and theme variable checks.

  • 'log': Log errors, skip invalid classes, continue
  • 'throw': Fail the render with every error it found, failing the build

A logged diagnostic is logged once while it persists - a dev server or watch mode re-rendering on each edit doesn't repeat it - and again if it goes away and comes back.

type "log" | "throw"

default 'throw' in CI (`CI` set to anything but empty, `false`, or `0`), 'log' otherwise

on_warning?

How to handle warnings during generation.

  • 'log': Log warnings, continue (once while each persists, like errors)
  • 'throw': Fail the render with every warning it found, failing the build
  • 'ignore': Suppress warnings entirely

type "log" | "throw" | "ignore"

default 'log'

import type {CssLiteralParseResult} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_literal.js';

Result of parsing a CSS-literal class name.

Uses a discriminated union (Result type) because parsing a single class is binary: it either succeeds or fails entirely. This differs from ExtractionResult which uses embedded diagnostics because file extraction can partially succeed (some classes extracted, others have errors).

Uses | null for diagnostics to avoid allocating empty arrays. Callers should use a guard pattern: if (result.diagnostics) { ... }

CssOutputOptions
#

css_plugin_options.ts view source

CssOutputOptions import type {CssOutputOptions} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_plugin_options.js';

Options for CSS output generation (theme + base + utilities). Controls how the three CSS layers are combined.

base_css?

Base styles (element defaults) configuration.

  • undefined (default): Use default style.css
  • null: Disable base styles entirely
  • string: Custom CSS to replace defaults
  • (default_css) => string: Callback to modify default CSS

The stylesheet is any CSS the parser accepts (parseCss from svelte/compiler), which the generator places in the fuz.base cascade layer, below themes and utility classes:

  • Top-level style rules and top-level @media, @supports, and @container rules are tree-shaken by the elements and classes they target. A conditional rule ships whole or not at all. Rules that target :root, :host, html, body, or * always ship, and so does a rule with a selector that can't be matched against detected usage: one naming no element or class ([role='button'], ::selection), or with an escaped or non-ASCII name (.md\:flex).
  • Every other at-rule ships as written (@keyframes, @font-face, @property, @scope, ...), used or not.
  • Every var() reference in CSS that ships is tracked, however deeply it is nested, so the theme includes the variables it needs.
  • The generator owns layering. A callback's additions land in fuz.base with everything else, so they lose to themes, utility classes, and unlayered styles - put overrides that must win in your own stylesheet. Top-level @layer fuz.base and @layer fuz.preferences blocks are recognized as the default stylesheet uses them; any other @layer rule is the error base_css_layer.
  • @import and @namespace are invalid inside a layer and are the error base_css_unsupported_at_rule.

An error never removes CSS: the construct ships as written (a layer becomes a sublayer of fuz.base, and browsers ignore the other two), and the error names it and its line. The one construct left out is a top-level @charset, which means nothing in a string. A stylesheet the parser rejects, or a callback that doesn't return a string, fails generation with an error naming base_css.

type BaseCssOption

// Append custom reset base_css: (css) => css + '\n\n* { box-sizing: border-box; }' // Prepend custom styles base_css: (css) => '.my-reset { margin: 0; }\n\n' + css

variables?

Theme variables configuration.

  • undefined (default): Use default variables from fuz_css
  • null: Disable theme entirely
  • Array<StyleVariable>: Custom variable definitions (replaces defaults)
  • (defaults) => Array<StyleVariable>: Callback to modify default variables

The set is the whole theme: only variables in it are emitted, and only the ones the output references. Base styles that reference a variable the fuz_css defaults define but this set lacks - with null, an empty array, or an array or callback result missing some - raise the error undefined_theme_variables, because a var() with no fallback would resolve to nothing. A reference with a fallback (var(--x, 1px)) is never an error, nor is a name the base styles declare themselves: in the rule that references it, or in a top-level rule with a selector that is exactly :root, :host, html, body, or *. Custom property names of your own are never checked.

To fix the error, define the variables here (keep the defaults a callback receives unless you replace what they style), or set base_css: null too for utility-only mode. To pair bundled base styles with a theme stylesheet imported separately, tell the generator the default set is defined elsewhere through exclude_variables.

type VariablesOption

// Override specific variables variables: (defaults) => defaults.map(v => v.name === 'hue_a' ? { ...v, base: '30' } : v ) // Add custom variables variables: (defaults) => [ ...defaults, { name: 'my_brand', base: '#ff6600', dark: '#ff8833' } ] // Bundled base styles over a separately imported `theme.css` variables: null, exclude_variables: default_variables.map((v) => v.name)

theme?

A theme to bake into the generated CSS, overlaid onto variables last-wins by name. This is how a project picks a theme statically: no JS theme rendering at runtime, and the output stays tree-shaken because the overlay happens before the dependency graph is built, so a theme's referenced variables are pulled in transitively.

For runtime switching use fuz_ui's ThemeRoot; the two compose, with the runtime theme winning by cascade layer. The theme's own overlay also renders into the fuz.theme.baked sublayer - above the fuz.preferences OS mappings, with color-scheme pinned for a stance, and below a runtime theme's direct fuz.theme styles - so the baked theme behaves like the same theme at runtime until one overrides it.

The bake derives what the theme renders with, as render_theme_style takes it at runtime, so a plain Theme is all it needs (a ResolvedTheme is accepted too, its derived data recomputed):

  • a single-scheme theme's stance mirror, re-slotted from the configured variables, so a customized scheme-adaptive variable keeps its own value under the stance
  • compiled chroma caps: compute_theme_caps recomputes the gamut caps wherever the theme's hues or lightness moved off the baked table (a rotated hue, a monochrome collapse), and the caps render last. The gates run with them and report as warnings - theme_gate_failed and theme_gate_unchecked - measured against the shipped defaults' numeric twin with the configured variables' knob-tier values folded in where they differ from the defaults, so the caps and gates measure what renders. A stanced theme lists only its stanced scheme's entries. A theme can fail a gate knowingly: marquee bakes with a gamut warning, since it exceeds the caps on purpose
  • the lint: validate_theme runs over the theme, each issue a theme_lint diagnostic at its own level - an unknown variable is an error, the knob range and type checks are warnings

The baked values become the output's defaults, so a runtime theme can't revert to the pre-bake appearance by being empty - the base theme renders nothing. To offer "back to fuz defaults" at runtime, render the defaults explicitly, internal ramp variables included: render_style_variables(default_variables).

type Theme | ResolvedTheme | null

import {phosphor_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/phosphor.ts'; vite_plugin_fuz_css({theme: phosphor_theme});

additional_classes?

Classes to always include in the output, regardless of detection. Useful for dynamically generated class names that can't be statically extracted. A class no class definition resolves is an error, as with a @fuz-classes hint, unless base styles are bundled and a base style rule targets it (like selected or palette_a).

type Iterable<string, any, any>

additional_elements?

Additional HTML elements to always include base styles for. Use 'all' to include all base styles regardless of detection. Useful for elements generated at runtime via document.createElement().

type Iterable<string, any, any> | "all"

additional_variables?

Additional CSS variables to always include in theme output. Use 'all' to include all theme variables regardless of detection. Useful for variables referenced dynamically.

type Iterable<string, any, any> | "all"

exclude_classes?

Classes to exclude from the output, even if detected. Useful for filtering out false positives from extraction.

type Iterable<string, any, any>

exclude_elements?

Elements to exclude from base CSS output, even if detected. Useful for filtering out elements you don't want styles for.

type Iterable<string, any, any>

exclude_variables?

CSS variables to exclude from theme output, even if referenced. Useful for filtering out variables you don't want in the theme, and for declaring that something else defines one: an excluded variable leaves out the dependencies only it pulls in, excluding one the output references or a shipped variable depends on is a warning when the theme has it, and a name listed here is skipped by the undefined_theme_variables check.

type Iterable<string, any, any>

// every default variable is defined by a stylesheet imported separately exclude_variables: default_variables.map((v) => v.name)

import {default_themes} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes.js';

The curated theme registry that theme pickers enumerate.

Registry themes are semantic-tier by policy: they move intent bindings (which palette letter a meaning points at) and levers (chroma scale, curves, form knobs) but never the palette hues themselves, so the letters stay a stable vocabulary across every registered theme.

Themes live one module per theme under themes/ and every module ships as an importable export - registry membership, not file location, is what separates registered themes from shipped exemplars. The registry holds the plain working themes: the base and themes/ledger.ts (compact, cool, for tools used all day).

The exemplars deliberately stay out of this list. Each takes one channel to carry the structure and quiets the rest, and is named for the artifact that already looks that way: themes/zine.ts (line and weight), themes/pebble.ts (depth and softness), themes/parchment.ts (type and ruling), themes/phosphor.ts (packing, dark-only), themes/guestbook.ts (controls as beveled objects), themes/marquee.ts (color, dark-only and the one palette-tier exemplar), and themes/signage.ts (scale and weight, for legibility).

Contrast is not a theme: the low/high contrast pair are modifiers (contrast_modifiers) composed over any theme with compose_themes.

escape_css_identifier
#

css_containment.ts view source

(value: string): string import {escape_css_identifier} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_containment.js';

Serializes a string as a CSS identifier, so any string can name an element id in a selector ('#' + escape_css_identifier(id) matches the element whose id attribute is that string). Follows the CSSOM identifier serialization, except that ASCII punctuation is escaped by code point (\3c ) rather than with a bare backslash, since \</style still closes a <style> element - the output can't end its rule or its element.

value

the raw identifier text

type string

returns

string

the identifier, safe to follow # or . in a selector

escape_css_selector
#

css_class_generation.ts view source

(name: string): string import {escape_css_selector} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_generation.js';

Escapes special characters in a CSS class name for use in a selector. ASCII punctuation like :, %, (, and ) takes a bare backslash, as does a space, which would otherwise split the selector in two; a leading digit (also after a leading -) and control characters take a hex escape, since neither is valid there as written, and NUL becomes U+FFFD.

name

type string

returns

string

examples

escape_css_selector('display:flex') // 'display\\:flex' escape_css_selector('opacity:80%') // 'opacity\\:80\\%' escape_css_selector('nth-child(2n)') // 'nth-child\\(2n\\)' escape_css_selector('2xl:p_md') // '\\32 xl\\:p_md'

FUZ_LAYER_ORDER_STATEMENT
#

theme.ts view source

"@layer fuz.base, fuz.preferences, fuz.theme, fuz.utilities;" import {FUZ_LAYER_ORDER_STATEMENT} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme.js';

The fuz_css cascade layer order: defaults (variables + element styles) in fuz.base, OS user-preference mappings (prefers-contrast, prefers-reduced-motion) in fuz.preferences, theme overrides in fuz.theme, generated utility classes in fuz.utilities. Layer order beats specificity and source order, so the preference mappings win over the defaults, theme overrides win over both regardless of head insertion order, and consumers' unlayered styles beat everything.

Two deliberate exceptions, both !important declarations in a layer, which outrank every later layer and unlayered styles: the prefers-reduced-motion mapping (a theme's durations must not re-enable motion the user turned off) and [hidden].

GATE_LINK
#

theme_check.ts view source

4.5 import {GATE_LINK} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_check.js';

AA links: --link_color (the accent at stop 60 by default) on shade_00, plus that stop itself when a theme repoints the role, since label.selected paints it directly, and an authored --link_color_selected.

GATE_PALETTE_TEXT
#

theme_check.ts view source

4.5 import {GATE_PALETTE_TEXT} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_check.js';

AA colored labels: every palette hue at stop 60 on shade_00 (colored text) and on its own stop-10 tint (the chip), and the .palette_X button label - the hue at stop 70 - on each of the button's fills. The fills follow the style.css recipe: the hue at stop 60 at 8% alpha at rest (and focused), 16% hovered, and 24% pressed, composited over shade_00 in gamma-encoded sRGB. A hovered label mixes 10% toward shade_max in oklab, so a mouse press pairs that label with the pressed fill, and a keyboard press, which doesn't hover, pairs the plain label with it. An 8-bit raster quantizes both colors, so a rendered measurement lands within about 0.15 of the ratio, and the gate reads it low more often than high.

GATE_SELECTED_TEXT
#

theme_check.ts view source

4.5 import {GATE_SELECTED_TEXT} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_check.js';

AA selected-control inverse text: text_00 on shade_60 and on every stop-60 fill - the selected-button pairings in style.css (.selected fills with shade_60, .palette_X.selected with palette_X_60). The endpoint stop is immune to text_lightness_curve bends, so this gate moves only when a theme moves the endpoints, the fill ramps, or the hues.

generate_classes_css
#

css_class_generation.ts view source

(options: GenerateClassesCssOptions): GenerateClassesCssResult import {generate_classes_css} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_generation.js';

Generates the utility CSS for a set of class names, wrapped in the fuz.utilities cascade layer.

Each class resolves to a structured rule - a definition plus the modifiers stripped from its name - and the emitted order comes from that structure, not from what the names say: composites render in the fuz.utilities.composites sublayer beneath every single-purpose class, and within each tier rules sort by color scheme, then media query (compare_media_modifiers), then property rank (shorthands before longhands, to_property_rank; definition order for composites), then state order (LVFHA), then the late flag (a late class after the rules it ties with), then registry order (interpreted classes after static ones), and only then by name, between interpreted classes of equal rank. Rules sharing a color scheme and media query render in one block. dark: and light: add no specificity (:where()), so they win by that order, and follow the OS preference when the root names no scheme (render_color_scheme_rules).

options

type GenerateClassesCssOptions

returns

GenerateClassesCssResult

The theme itself was already baked into resources' variable graph, which carries it with its derived mirror and caps, and that baked theme is what re-renders into the fuz.theme cascade layer (above the fuz.preferences OS mappings, with a stance's color-scheme pin), matching how the same theme behaves at runtime.

guestbook_theme
#

themes/guestbook.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {guestbook_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/guestbook.js';

An exemplar theme: the guestbook of a 90s homepage. Structure comes from controls drawn as objects - sunken fields under raised buttons that press to inset, the bevel doing the work shadows do elsewhere. Colorless system chrome on a ground that sits off the paper-white extreme, one serif family for everything the way the browser default was, square corners, packed dense, and links underlined at rest. Sits between ledger's compact and phosphor's terminal density.

The proof that --button_border_style/--button_border_style_active express a raised/pressed pair. Dual-scheme: by night the same chrome in slate, the hi-color desktop after dark. Built from levers only - the palette letters keep their default hues, and nothing is pushed past the gamut caps.

high_contrast_theme
#

themes/high_contrast.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {high_contrast_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/high_contrast.js';

Stretched contrast: a pure white page background in light mode and a deepened one in dark, text bent toward the contrast end - curve-knob moves, not stop surgery - darker links, and stronger borders.

The dark ground stops short of pure black because the bottom of the lightness range carries almost no luminance: going to black buys text a sliver of contrast while collapsing the surface steps and weakening borders. The text bend is moderate for a similar reason - the stretched ground already takes body text past AAA, and a harder bend lifts disabled and subtle text to nearly body contrast, flattening the hierarchy those stops encode.

On the white ground an input's sunken fill has nowhere to go, so the border alone marks a control, and it moves up the shade ramp to stay past 3:1 against the page. Panels get a ring in that border color, since their faint fill reads as nothing beside the louder text and borders - which replaces a theme's own panel_shadow while the modifier holds.

ledger_theme
#

themes/ledger.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {ledger_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/ledger.js';

The working theme: the ledger. For tools used all day - a cool gray whisper in the neutral, color eased down so status reads without shouting, compact spacing and leading (visibly tighter than the base, so the registry's two entries read as two choices), one sans family, a flatter type scale, and restrained corners and depth. Plain on purpose: no decoration, no clipped gamut, the default accent.

Dual-scheme and semantic-tier - it moves levers only, so the palette letters keep their hues and it sits in the registry beside the base theme.

low_contrast_theme
#

themes/low_contrast.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {low_contrast_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/low_contrast.js';

Gentle contrast: a compressed surface range, tuned to the softest compression that still clears the check_theme text, link, border, and fill gates over the base theme. Composed over a theme with a tighter ground it can dip below a gate, so check the composition.

It moves the ground and nothing else, so a theme keeps its own neutral cast under it.

marquee_theme
#

themes/marquee.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {marquee_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/marquee.js';

An exemplar theme: the theater marquee at night. Color is the content - a magenta accent over a deep purple-cast dark, shadows turned to cyan and magenta glows, corners rounded onto a common floor like tube bends. Vivid past the gamut caps on purpose - lightness holds through the clipping, so check_theme reports gamut failures and baking it through the build-time theme option warns with them. Dark-only via the scheme stance: a lit sign has no daytime appearance, so it renders through resolve_theme_stance, which computes the stance mirror beside it.

The one palette-tier exemplar: it rotates the yellow slot to the amber of incandescent bulbs, so a letter hue itself moves - the move that keeps a theme out of the semantic-tier registry.

PALETTE_CHROMA_CAPS
#

ramps.ts view source

Readonly<Record<"dark" | "light", Readonly<Record<"00" | "05" | "10" | "20" | "30" | "40" | "50" | "60" | "70" | "80" | "90" | "95" | "100", number>>>>

type Readonly<Record<ColorSchemeVariant, Readonly<Record<NumericScaleVariant, number>>>>

import {PALETTE_CHROMA_CAPS} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Worst-hue safe chroma caps per stop: the largest chroma at that stop's default lightness that stays inside sRGB for every default hue (see oklch_max_srgb_chroma for the non-convexity caveat). Computed at design time from PALETTE_HUES + PALETTE_LIGHTNESS_KNOBS, floored to stay conservative; a drift test recomputes them from the color math.

PALETTE_CHROMA_KNOBS
#

ramps.ts view source

Readonly<Record<"dark" | "light", Readonly<ChromaRampKnobs>>>

type Readonly<Record<ColorSchemeVariant, Readonly<ChromaRampKnobs>>>

import {PALETTE_CHROMA_KNOBS} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Fitted chroma-curve knobs for the palette ramps. curve renders as the single --chroma_curve, which the neutral scales share; chroma_min and chroma_max are the palette's own.

Fitted so the requested curve hugs the effective post-clamp chroma instead of sitting above the caps through the mid-range - turning the knobs down responds immediately. Turning chroma_max up remains cap-clamped by design; --chroma_scale is the push-past-the-gamut knob. The residual vs the HSL palette this fit ports is small (mean ΔEOK ≈ 0.005 light / 0.003 dark) except light stop 30 (−0.028 C): the symmetric mid-peaked model can't reach the light cap envelope's peak there - recovering it would take an asymmetric shape (a peak-position knob).

PALETTE_CHROMA_MULTIPLIERS
#

ramps.ts view source

Readonly<Record<"a" | "b" | "c" | "d" | "e" | "f" | "g" | "h" | "i" | "j", number>>

type Readonly<Record<PaletteVariant, number>>

import {PALETTE_CHROMA_MULTIPLIERS} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

Per-slot chroma multipliers (--palette_X_chroma_scale), the palette's chroma-character knobs. Each multiplies its slot's chroma under the global --chroma_scale (multiplicative, so the slot's character is preserved at any global setting); values at or below 1 stay inside the worst-hue gamut caps by construction, above 1 knowingly clips like the global knob. The brown slot ships muted because brown is low-chroma dark orange - no hue angle renders it at full palette chroma.

parchment_theme
#

themes/parchment.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {parchment_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/parchment.js';

An exemplar theme: the manuscript page. Structure comes from type and ruling - serif body text on warm parchment surfaces (the neutral's default brown binding, tinted up), rubrication-red accents the way scribes marked emphasis, and double-ruled frames. Chroma eases below 1 for aged pigment, the page rather than its illumination.

Dual-scheme: the dark appearance is the same page by candlelight, the ground deepening to tanned leather and the ink warming to cream rather than white. The material reads in both, so it takes no scheme stance - a dark-mode reader who picks it isn't flashed a lit page.

parse_css_literal

css_literal.ts view source

(class_name: string, css_properties: Set<string> | null): CssLiteralParseResult import {parse_css_literal} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_literal.js';

Parses a CSS-literal class name into its components.

The value renders verbatim, so one that could end its declaration or rule (an unclosed quote or bracket, a stray ), a top-level ;) is an error: it must pass css_value_is_contained once a trailing !important is split off. That check is stricter than the CSS grammar - it also rejects braces, comments, and escapes outside strings (--x:{}, content:\201C), any ! but that trailing one (display:flex!, color:red!important!important), and an unquoted url( holding what needs quotes - so quote such values or set them in a stylesheet. The property name renders verbatim too, so it must pass is_valid_css_property, which holds a custom property's name to a plain identifier.

class_name

the class name to parse

type string

css_properties

Set of valid CSS properties from load_css_properties() Pass null to skip property validation.

type Set<string> | null

parse_style_css

style_rule_parser.ts view source

(css: string): StyleRuleIndex import {parse_style_css} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/style_rule_parser.js';

Parses a base stylesheet into a StyleRuleIndex.

Each top-level style rule and at-rule becomes one indexed rule that ships whole or not at all. A top-level @layer fuz.base or `@layer fuz.preferences` block is unwrapped first, so its contents are top-level too and bundled output re-layers the selected rules; the shipped layer order statement is skipped because the bundle emits its own, and so is @charset, which means nothing in a string. Every other @layer rule, and each @import/@namespace, becomes an error in the index's diagnostics and is still indexed as written - an error never removes CSS.

css

raw CSS string (e.g., contents of style.css)

returns

pebble_theme
#

themes/pebble.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {pebble_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/pebble.js';

An exemplar theme: the river pebble. Structure comes from depth and softness - round corners, worn to pills on the controls, controls that sit raised on a soft drop shadow and press inward, panels that lift a little off the page, and generous spacing. A cool gray whisper in the neutral and one sans family at a semibold heading weight.

Dual-scheme: in dark the drop falls into the shadow_color_shroud black while the top edge catches a little light. Built from levers only - the palette letters keep their default hues, and nothing is pushed past the gamut caps.

phosphor_theme
#

themes/phosphor.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {phosphor_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/phosphor.js';

An exemplar theme: the green-phosphor CRT terminal. Structure comes from packing - monospace, sharp-cornered, spacing and leading packed well past the compact themes, and a type scale flattened nearly to one size, with bold headings carrying the hierarchy, give it terminal density, and the three shortest duration tokens are zero. The phosphor tint carries the surfaces and accent, but the palette slots keep their own hues so status colors still read - negative stays red, caution amber, info cyan, and positive steps over to teal so a success never reads as a link.

The screen emits rather than reflects: the ground is the gray-green of an unlit tube face, lifted off black so a surface can still sink below it, and controls glow where other themes cast shadows. Dark-only via the scheme stance: a CRT has no daytime appearance, so it renders through resolve_theme_stance, which computes the stance mirror beside it.

render_theme_style
#

theme.ts view source

(theme: { name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }, options?: RenderThemeStyleOptions): string import {render_theme_style} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme.js';

Renders a theme's variables as CSS, wrapped in the fuz.theme cascade layer by default.

Renders exactly what the theme carries plus the derived data in options: the stance mirror (under a stance only, minus any name the theme or the caps set), then the theme's variables, then the caps. An empty theme renders nothing (inheriting the fuz.base defaults) unless a scheme stance needs pinning. To render a single-scheme theme faithfully, resolve it first and pass the result as the options: render_theme_style(resolved.theme, resolved).

A theme can't set the internal ramp variables, so a _-prefixed name in theme.variables is dropped - the schema rejects one, and this holds the same line for a theme that skipped it. The derived scheme_mirror and caps carry internal names by design and render them. To render a variable set that isn't a theme, like the full defaults, use render_style_variables.

Total over any JSON value in either argument, because a theme restored from storage reaches this without passing the schema: whatever isn't the type declared is dropped instead of thrown on or coerced into the stylesheet. A variables, scheme_mirror, or caps that isn't an array renders as empty, an entry that isn't an object is skipped, a name or slot that isn't a contained string drops its declaration, and a summary that isn't one drops its comment (see css_containment.ts).

theme

the theme to render

type Theme

options

see RenderThemeStyleOptions

type RenderThemeStyleOptions
default {}

returns

string

the theme CSS, or an empty string when there's nothing to render

RenderStyleVariablesOptions
#

theme.ts view source

RenderStyleVariablesOptions import type {RenderStyleVariablesOptions} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme.js';

comments?

type boolean

id?

Scopes the rendered variables to #id instead of :root. Dark slots render for both placements of the scheme class - on the scope element itself (#id.dark) and on the root (:root.dark #id), the ecosystem convention - so a scoped theme's dark appearance follows the page's. A .light on the scope element wins over either: the scope takes the theme's base slots under :root.dark and on a dark OS alike. With no scheme class on the root or the scope, the dark slots follow the OS preference.

Only literal-valued variables take effect in a scope: the derived color stops (--palette_a_50, --shade_50, ...) resolve their calc() on :root, and a descendant inherits the computed color, so a curve knob like --chroma_scale set at #id changes nothing. Knob-only themes need :root.

Any string works: it's escaped into the selector, so it matches the element whose id attribute is that string and can't end the rule or the <style> element. An empty string renders to :root.

type string | null

layer?

The cascade layer wrapping the rendered variables. Theme overrides default to fuz.theme so they beat the fuz.base defaults by layer order; pass null to render unlayered. A value that isn't a dotted layer name (fuz.theme.baked) falls back to the default.

type string | null

Resolves an array of class names to their combined CSS declarations.

Recursively resolves nested composes arrays and combines all declarations. Validates that referenced classes exist and are resolvable (not rulesets or interpreters). Supports unmodified CSS literals (e.g., text-align:center) in the composes array.

Deduplication behavior:

  • Diamond dependencies (class reached via different composition branches) are silently skipped
  • Redundant listings (class already included by an earlier sibling in this array) emit a warning

scheme_stance_variables
#

theme_stance.ts view source

(scheme: "dark" | "light", variables?: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]): { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[] import {scheme_stance_variables} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_stance.js';

Computes the mirror a single-scheme stance implies: every scheme-adaptive variable in variables (those carrying a dark slot), re-slotted with the stanced scheme's value in the base slot. A base-slot declaration in fuz.theme applies in both color schemes - cascade-layer order beats the higher specificity of the fuz.base dark-scheme defaults (:root.dark and its prefers-color-scheme twin) - and keeping the mirror out of the dark slot means later same-block declarations (the theme's own variables, composed overlays, compiled caps) always win by source order.

The mirror depends on the stance alone, not on the theme: the renderer skips an entry whose name the theme or its caps set.

type "light" | "dark"

variables

the variable set to mirror, scheme_adaptive_variables by default

SHADE_CHROMA_00
#

ramps.ts view source

0 import {SHADE_CHROMA_00} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

The ground's own chroma (--shade_chroma_00), added to the near-ground stops of the shade ramp by neutral_ground_chroma_weight. The chroma shape is 0 at the endpoints, so without it the page ground is untinted whatever neutral_chroma says; a theme whose identity is a tinted page (paper, a lit night) sets it. 0 keeps the default ground neutral.

SHADE_GROUND_CHROMA_REACH
#

ramps.ts view source

0.5 import {SHADE_GROUND_CHROMA_REACH} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/ramps.js';

How far up the shade ramp the ground's chroma reaches, as a ramp position (0 is the ground, 1 the far end): the tint is whole at shade_00 and gone by this stop. The near-ground stops are the surfaces raised off the page - sidebars, fills, wells - and the shared chroma shape is near 0 there too, so without the reach they read gray beside a tinted ground.

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {signage_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/signage.js';

An exemplar theme: built for legibility, the way public signage is - read at a distance, in passing, by anyone. Structure comes from scale and weight: generous spacing, larger body text, an opened-up type scale, a heavier body weight under bold grotesque headings at normal tracking, thick borders, flat fields, underlined links, and a focus ring too wide to miss. The palette stays at the gamut caps: signage color is saturated but it has to print.

For public-facing sites, older readers, kiosks, and anyone who wants the defaults turned up rather than restyled. Dual-scheme, and the one exemplar whose accent changes between them: by day the wayfinding blue of a printed board, by night the yellow of a lit departure display. Built from levers only - the palette letters keep their default hues.

splice_css_at_placeholder
#

css_placeholder_splice.ts view source

(source: string, generated_css: string): string | null import {splice_css_at_placeholder} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_placeholder_splice.js';

Replaces the first placeholder in a bundled stylesheet with the generated CSS, at the offset the marker occupies.

Position is the point: the marker sits where Vite placed virtual:fuz.css in the importer's stylesheet, so writing the generated CSS there reproduces the import order the source asked for. Appending to the end of the asset instead would silently move fuz_css's :root after every stylesheet bundled alongside it, so an app's own equal-specificity token override would win in dev (where the virtual module is served in place) and lose in the production bundle.

Usually the marker is its own rule, but a minifier that merges adjacent rules with identical selectors (lightningcss is one; esbuild, Vite's default, isn't) folds neighboring :root declarations into the marker's block - from either or both sides. Declaration order preserves the merged rules' order, so splitting the block at the marker keeps the cascade exact: declarations before it came from stylesheets bundled before virtual:fuz.css and stay before the generated CSS, declarations after it stay after. The solo-rule case is the same split with both sides empty.

The marker's rule starts after whatever ends the preceding construct: a rule's }, a statement at-rule's ; (@charset, @import, which a bundler hoists ahead of the first rule), or an enclosing block's {. Comments, strings, and unquoted url()s are read past, since one can hold any of those - an unminified build or a preserved /*! *\/ comment leaves them in, and a content string or a URL can hold a /* of its own.

source

the bundled stylesheet holding the marker

type string

generated_css

the CSS to write at the marker's position

type string

returns

string | null

source with the generated CSS spliced in and the marker stripped, or null if no marker sits inside a well-formed rule

StyleVariable
#

variable.ts view source

value + type

{ name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; } import {StyleVariable} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/variable.js';

A style variable: a custom property name with a value per color scheme.

The slots follow the renderer's cascade: base is the base position, rendered on :root, and dark renders on :root.dark (and for a root naming no scheme, under prefers-color-scheme: dark). A theme variable with only base therefore applies in both color schemes (its fuz.theme :root beats the fuz.base dark default by layer order), while dark alone applies in dark only - which is why the shipped themes author a scheme-agnostic knob as a single base value. The light scheme renders base; there is no light-only slot.

Strict: a misspelled slot is an error, not a silently dropped scheme. A slot must also be a contained CSS value (see css_containment.ts), since it renders verbatim.

The name is a public one (StyleVariableName): an internal ramp variable is rejected with an error saying so. The derived data that does carry internal names - a stance's mirror and compile_theme's caps - travels beside a theme as ThemeDerived, never inside it.

name

type string

dark?

type string

base?

type string

summary?

type string

theme.ts view source

ThemeDerived import type {ThemeDerived} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme.js';

Data derived from a theme rather than authored in it: what a theme's stance and hues imply, computed by resolve_theme_stance and compile_theme (theme_compile.ts) and handed to render_theme_style beside the theme. Never part of a Theme, so a persisted or shared theme can't carry stale derived values - it's recomputed from the theme wherever the theme renders, and never validated.

scheme_mirror?

The stance mirror: the scheme-adaptive variables re-slotted (the defaults' twin at runtime, the configured set at build time) into the base position with the stanced scheme's value, so a single-scheme theme's one appearance holds in both color schemes. Rendered first and only under a stance, skipping any name the theme's variables or the caps set.

type StyleVariable[]

caps?

Recomputed worst-hue chroma caps from compile_theme (or compute_theme_caps alone), as _palette_chroma_NN overrides. Rendered last, so they win over the mirror's re-slotted defaults.

type StyleVariable[]

internal

Exported for its tests.

(id: string): string import {to_extraction_id} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/vite_plugin_fuz_css.js';

Converts a Vite module id to the id its extraction is keyed by, dropping a query made only of Vite's cache-busting parameters - the v version hash the dev server gives a dependency's URL and the t HMR timestamp. Such an id is the file itself, so it's filtered, parsed, cached, and deleted as the plain path, sharing one entry with the same file's SSR transform and pre-scan.

Any other query is kept, because it names a different module than the file: Foo.svelte?svelte&type=style&lang.css is the component's CSS, and ?raw, ?url, and ?worker ids carry a generated wrapper rather than the file's source.

the id without its query when that query only busts a cache, otherwise id unchanged

css_class_generation.ts view source

(property: string): number import {to_property_rank} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/css_class_generation.js';

The cascade rank of a CSS property, so a shorthand emits before the longhands it sets and a longhand class wins where both apply: the depth of its name (padding 0, padding-left 1, border-top-color 2), vendor prefix ignored, with SHORTHAND_RANKS for the shorthands whose longhands don't extend their name. Custom properties rank 0. Properties that aren't shorthand-related can share a rank harmlessly - they never overlap.

property

type string

returns

number

validate_theme
#

theme_validate.ts view source

(theme: unknown): ThemeIssue[] import {validate_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/theme_validate.js';

Lints a theme's structure: the Theme schema (errors), a known name per variable (errors, with a warning instead for a contextual hook from style_hooks.ts, which a theme shouldn't set), and advisory type/range warnings for the knob-tier variables - including a pairing warning when an intent hue binds a palette letter whose chroma multiplier differs from the intent's own *_chroma_scale twin (a binding shares only the hue angle, so the slot's chroma character is otherwise silently dropped), and a separation warning when the accent hue lands within ACCENT_STATUS_HUE_SEPARATION of a status hue. Value validation is advisory and never an error. An empty array means the theme is structurally valid.

A shape failure returns on its own: the knob lint reads values the schema hasn't vouched for, so it runs only over a theme that parsed. Takes unknown so untrusted input (a theme restored from storage, a pasted object) needs no cast to be checked.

theme

type unknown

Type for the variables option used by the generator.

Supports four forms:

  • undefined - Use default variables (framework defaults)
  • null - Disable theme generation entirely (explicit opt-out)
  • Array<StyleVariable> - Custom variables array (replaces defaults)
  • (defaults) => Array<StyleVariable> - Callback to modify defaults

See module documentation for the undefined vs null convention.

the plugin as several objects sharing state, to pass to Vite's plugins together: an enforce: 'pre' one that does the extraction, serves the virtual module, and splices the build's CSS ahead of other plugins, a build-only one positioned after Vite's CSS processing that completes the build's stylesheets, and a serve-only enforce: 'post' one that adds the evaluation report to the virtual module's client code

VitePluginFuzCssOptions
#

vite_plugin_fuz_css.ts view source

VitePluginFuzCssOptions import type {VitePluginFuzCssOptions} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/vite_plugin_fuz_css.js';

Options for the fuz_css Vite plugin. Extends the shared base options with Vite-specific options.

inheritance

extends: CssGeneratorBaseOptions

prescan?

Dev-only eager pre-scan of source files at server startup.

Extraction state accumulates from Vite's transform hook, so without a pre-scan the first CSS served on a cold start includes only the files the module graph happened to visit first, and the rest arrives as corrective HMR updates while the page loads. The pre-scan extracts every file passing filter_file under the given directories, plus the Vite root's index.html, before the virtual module is first served, so the initial CSS is complete. Warm starts are cheap via the extraction cache.

true scans src under the Vite root; false disables; an array gives custom directories (resolved against the Vite root unless absolute). The root index.html is included whichever directories are given: the dev server serves it without running transform on it, so nothing else would extract it. Pre-scanned files are kept current - one the watcher reports added or changed is extracted again, whether or not any module imports it.

node_modules dependencies are never pre-scanned, and neither are project files outside the scanned directories. They're extracted when the dev server first transforms them, which is during the first load of a page that uses them, so that page's CSS is completed by an update a moment after it's first served rather than up front (or by the next reload, with server.hmr or server.ws off).

What dev and build extract differs at the edges:

  • dev only: files under the scanned directories that no module imports (SvelteKit's src/app.html among them), including ones imported only with ?raw - the pre-scan reads them from disk, where a build extracts just the modules it transforms; and a pre-bundled dependency that's extracted from its bundled code while filter_file rejects the files it ships (the default filter skips .mjs), which a build doesn't extract at all
  • build only: an HTML entry outside the scanned directories other than the root index.html; a module of a pre-bundled dependency that the pre-bundler dropped as unused, such as one holding nothing but a @fuz-classes comment; and the comment hints and static Svelte class attributes of a pre-bundled dependency whose sourcemap is missing or names files that aren't installed, which is extracted from its bundled code instead

type boolean | string[]

default true

zine_theme
#

themes/zine.ts view source

{ name: string; variables: { name: string; dark?: string | undefined; base?: string | undefined; summary?: string | undefined; }[]; summary?: string | undefined; scheme?: "dark" | "light" | "dual" | undefined; }

type Theme

import {zine_theme} from '@fuzdev/fuz_css/themes/zine.js';

An exemplar theme: the photocopied zine. Structure comes from line and weight alone, since that is all a photocopier reproduces - paper white and toner black with no gray between them, thick opaque borders, square corners, no shadows, heavy grotesque headings set tight, links marked by an underline. The three shortest duration tokens are zero, since print doesn't ease. The palette keeps its full chroma, the spot color run over the black plate.

Dual-scheme: the dark appearance is the same page run as a negative, on a near-black ground that stays inside the contrast modifiers' range, so high contrast still deepens it and panels keep a visible fill. Built from levers only - the palette letters keep their default hues.
